questions.q: A 35-year-old farmer presents with a painless ulcer on the right hand with regional lymphadenopathy. Culture reveals gram-positive rod-shaped organisms arranged in chains forming 'medusa head' colonies on blood agar. What is the most appropriate treatment?
questions.exp: Cutaneous anthrax caused by Bacillus anthracis is treated with ciprofloxacin 500mg BD for 60 days (or until bioterrorism exposure ruled out). Penicillin was traditional but fluoroquinolones are now preferred due to engineered resistance concerns.

questions.q: A 28-year-old male presents with a painful genital ulcer with undermined edges and unilateral tender inguinal lymphadenopathy. Gram stain of the ulcer discharge shows 'school of fish' or 'railway track' pattern of gram-negative rods. The causative organism is:
questions.exp: Chancroid caused by Haemophilus ducreyi presents as a painful ulcer with the characteristic 'school of fish' pattern on Gram stain. Painful ulcer with tender lymphadenopathy distinguishes it from syphilis (painless). Treatment: azithromycin 1g single dose or ceftriaxone 250mg IM.

questions.q: A 45-year-old patient from a leprosy-endemic area presents with hypopigmented patches on the trunk. Slit skin smear shows AFB with BI of 4+. Histopathology shows foamy macrophages (Virchow cells) with no lymphocytic infiltrate. This patient should receive:
questions.exp: BI of 4+ and Virchow cells (foam cells/lepra cells) with no lymphocyte response indicates lepromatous leprosy — a multibacillary (MB) type. WHO MB-MDT (rifampicin 600mg monthly + clofazimine 300mg monthly + 50mg daily + dapsone 100mg daily) is given for 12 months.

questions.q: A 22-year-old woman presents with recurrent oral ulcers, genital ulcers, and uveitis. She also has a positive pathergy test. The HLA type most associated with her diagnosis is:
questions.exp: Behçet's disease (triple symptom complex: oral ulcers, genital ulcers, uveitis) with positive pathergy test is strongly associated with HLA-B51. It is most prevalent in Turkey, Middle East, and Japan along the ancient Silk Route.

questions.q: A 55-year-old patient presents with tense bullae on normal-appearing skin, predominantly on the lower abdomen and thighs. Direct immunofluorescence shows linear IgG and C3 along the basement membrane zone. The target antigen is:
questions.exp: Bullous pemphigoid (BP) presents with tense bullae in elderly, predominantly on flexural areas. DIF shows linear IgG and C3 at BMZ. The target antigens are BPAG1 (BP230) and BPAG2 (BP180/type XVII collagen). Desmoglein 1/3 are targets in pemphigus.

questions.q: A 40-year-old HIV-positive patient (CD4 count 50 cells/μL) presents with violaceous papules and nodules on the lower extremities and palate. Biopsy shows spindle cell proliferation with slit-like vascular spaces and extravasated red blood cells. The causative agent is:
questions.exp: AIDS-related Kaposi sarcoma is caused by Human Herpesvirus 8 (HHV-8/KSHV). It presents with violaceous lesions predominantly on lower extremities and oral mucosa in immunocompromised individuals. CD4 <200 is a risk factor. Treatment: HAART + local or systemic chemotherapy.

questions.q: A 30-year-old patient presents with tinea capitis showing black dots and broken hairs at follicular orifices. KOH examination shows endothrix spores within the hair shaft. The most common causative organism is:
questions.exp: Black dot tinea capitis shows endothrix invasion (spores within hair shaft, no fluorescence on Wood's lamp). Trichophyton tonsurans is the most common cause in the USA. T. violaceum is common in India. Microsporum species cause ectothrix and show Wood's lamp fluorescence.

questions.q: A 25-year-old presents with annular, serpiginous plaques with a raised scaly border on the trunk. The inner border heals while the outer border advances. What is the investigation of choice?
questions.exp: The described lesion is tinea corporis (ringworm) caused by dermatophytes. KOH (potassium hydroxide) mount examination of skin scrapings from the active border shows septate branching hyphae — the first-line investigation for dermatophytosis.

questions.q: A neonate presents on day 2 of life with vesicles clustered on an erythematous base on the scalp. Tzanck smear shows multinucleated giant cells. The most dangerous complication of this condition is:
questions.exp: Neonatal herpes simplex (HSV-2 predominantly) can disseminate causing encephalitis (mortality >80% if untreated). Tzanck smear showing multinucleated giant cells confirms herpesvirus. IV acyclovir 60mg/kg/day in 3 divided doses for 21 days is the treatment for disseminated/CNS disease.

questions.q: A 20-year-old woman presents with a photosensitive butterfly rash on the face, oral ulcers, and arthralgia. ANA titre is 1:640, anti-dsDNA positive. The most specific antibody for her diagnosis is:
questions.exp: Anti-Sm (anti-Smith) antibody is the MOST SPECIFIC antibody for SLE (specificity ~99%), though sensitivity is low (25-30%). Anti-dsDNA is also specific but anti-Sm is considered the most specific. ANA is sensitive but not specific. Anti-Ro is associated with neonatal lupus and subacute cutaneous LE.

questions.q: A 50-year-old male presents with Gottron's papules over the MCPJs and PIPJs, heliotrope rash, and proximal muscle weakness. The most dangerous systemic complication that determines prognosis is:
questions.exp: Dermatomyositis (DM) is associated with interstitial lung disease (ILD) in 20-30% of cases, and ILD is the most significant cause of morbidity and mortality. Anti-Jo-1 antibody is associated with the antisynthetase syndrome which includes ILD, myositis, and mechanic's hands. DM in adults is also associated with underlying malignancy.

questions.q: A 60-year-old farmer presents with a pearly, rolled-edged translucent nodule on the nose with telangiectasia. He works outdoors and has chronic sun exposure. The most appropriate treatment is:
questions.exp: Basal cell carcinoma (BCC) on the nose — a high-risk site — requires Mohs micrographic surgery (MMS) for the highest cure rate and tissue conservation. MMS achieves 5-year cure rates >99% for primary BCC. High-risk sites for BCC include face (H-zone), scalp, ears.

questions.q: A 35-year-old presents with a rapidly growing, firm, well-circumscribed nodule on the cheek that developed over 6 weeks, with a central keratin-filled crater. It is now regressing spontaneously. The most likely diagnosis is:
questions.exp: Keratoacanthoma (KA) is a rapidly growing keratinocytic lesion that classically develops over 4-6 weeks, reaches a stable phase, then spontaneously involutes over months. It presents with a central keratin-filled crater. Histologically similar to SCC — some consider it a low-grade SCC. Treatment is excision.

questions.q: A 45-year-old presents with a pigmented lesion on the sole with ABCDE criteria suggesting melanoma. Dermoscopy shows a parallel ridge pattern. The Breslow thickness on excision is 2.5mm. What is the recommended surgical margin?
questions.exp: For melanoma with Breslow thickness 1.01–2mm: 1-2cm margin is recommended. For thickness >2mm (like 2.5mm): 2cm margin is standard. Sentinel lymph node biopsy is recommended for Breslow >0.8mm or any ulcerated melanoma. Parallel ridge pattern on dermoscopy of acral skin is a hallmark of acral lentiginous melanoma.

questions.q: A 30-year-old pregnant woman in her third trimester presents with intensely pruritic urticarial papules and plaques confined to striae distensae on the abdomen, sparing the periumbilical area. The most likely diagnosis is:
opts: Pruritic urticarial papules and plaques of pregnancy (PUPPP)
questions.exp: PUPPP (polymorphic eruption of pregnancy) classically begins within striae on the abdomen, characteristically sparing the umbilicus. It occurs in primigravidas, usually in the third trimester. DIF is negative. Pemphigoid gestationis involves the periumbilical area and shows DIF positivity (C3 at BMZ).

questions.q: A 25-year-old develops painful erosions and crusting on the lips and mucosa, target lesions on palms, and systemic symptoms 2 weeks after starting trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole. Biopsy shows full-thickness epidermal necrosis with >30% BSA involvement. What is the most appropriate initial management?
opts: Withdraw offending drug and supportive burn unit care
questions.exp: Stevens-Johnson syndrome/Toxic Epidermal Necrolysis (SJS/TEN): epidermal detachment >30% = TEN. Immediate drug withdrawal is the most critical step. Management is supportive in a burn unit (fluid replacement, wound care, eye/airway care). IVIG and cyclosporine are used as adjuncts. Corticosteroids are controversial and generally avoided in TEN.

questions.q: During patch testing for allergic contact dermatitis, a patient shows a 2+ reaction at 48 hours and 72 hours to nickel sulfate. The 2+ reaction is defined as:
questions.exp: ICDRG patch test grading: + (1+) = erythema + infiltration; ++ (2+) = erythema + infiltration + papules + vesicles; +++ (3+) = bullous reaction; ? = doubtful (mild erythema only); IR = irritant reaction. The 2+ reaction indicates a true allergic reaction with papules and vesicles.

questions.q: A 20-year-old student presents with painful genital ulcer with a clean base. Dark-field microscopy of the exudate shows motile spirochetes. RPR and VDRL are non-reactive. The most likely explanation is:
opts: Primary syphilis within the first 2 weeks
questions.exp: In primary syphilis, serological tests (RPR/VDRL) may be non-reactive in the first 1-4 weeks after infection. Dark-field microscopy showing motile spirochetes is diagnostic at this early stage. The window period before seroconversion is an important concept — dark-field microscopy or PCR should be used in suspected early syphilis with negative serology.

questions.q: A 55-year-old woman presents with violaceous papules and plaques with Wickham's striae on the buccal mucosa and wrists. Biopsy shows saw-tooth rete ridges, hypergranulosis, and a band-like lymphocytic infiltrate at the dermo-epidermal junction with colloid bodies. The most common site of malignant transformation in this condition is:
questions.exp: Lichen planus (LP) has a risk of squamous cell carcinoma transformation, predominantly in oral LP (0.5-1% risk over 5 years), especially the erosive/ulcerative type. This is higher than cutaneous LP. Genital LP can also transform. Regular surveillance of oral LP is recommended.

questions.q: A leprosy patient on multidrug therapy develops painful, tender erythematous nodules on the face and trunk with fever and arthralgias. His BI was 4+ before treatment. This reaction is classified as:
questions.exp: Erythema Nodosum Leprosum (ENL) = Type 2 lepra reaction — occurs in MB leprosy (LL/BL), presenting as painful tender erythematous nodules with systemic symptoms. It is an immune complex-mediated reaction (Type III hypersensitivity). Treatment: thalidomide (most effective), corticosteroids, or clofazimine. MDT should be continued.

questions.q: A 35-year-old woman presents with Raynaud's phenomenon, sclerodactyly, telangiectasias, and esophageal dysmotility. Anti-centromere antibody is positive. She most likely has:
questions.exp: CREST syndrome (Calcinosis, Raynaud's, Esophageal dysmotility, Sclerodactyly, Telangiectasia) = limited cutaneous systemic sclerosis (lcSSc). Anti-centromere antibody (ACA) is the hallmark antibody, present in 70-80% of lcSSc. Anti-Scl-70 (anti-topoisomerase I) is associated with diffuse SSc and ILD.

questions.q: A 3-year-old child presents with honey-colored crusted lesions around the nose and mouth. Culture grows Staphylococcus aureus and Group A Streptococcus. The first-line systemic treatment is:
questions.exp: Non-bullous impetigo (most common form) in children is caused by S. aureus and/or Group A Streptococcus. Oral cephalexin (first-generation cephalosporin) is first-line systemic therapy. Topical mupirocin is used for localized disease. Amoxicillin-clavulanate is an alternative. Avoid amoxicillin alone as it doesn't cover S. aureus.

questions.q: A 40-year-old immunocompromised patient presents with verrucous plaques on the forearm that developed after a minor trauma. Biopsy shows sclerotic bodies (Medlar bodies/copper penny bodies). The most likely causative organism is:
questions.exp: Chromoblastomycosis presents as verrucous plaques typically on distal extremities. The hallmark is Medlar bodies (sclerotic bodies/copper penny bodies) on histopathology — dark brown, thick-walled, septate cells. Fonsecaea pedrosoi is the most common causative organism. Treatment: itraconazole ± terbinafine, cryosurgery.

questions.q: A patient is being treated with dapsone for dermatitis herpetiformis. After 4 weeks, the patient presents with cyanosis and fatigue. G6PD levels are normal. The most likely complication is:
questions.exp: Dapsone commonly causes methemoglobinemia and hemolytic anemia (even with normal G6PD). Methemoglobinemia presents with cyanosis, fatigue, and 'chocolate-brown' blood. Treatment: methylene blue 1-2mg/kg IV. G6PD deficiency worsens hemolysis. Dapsone hypersensitivity syndrome (DHS) occurs 5-6 weeks after initiation.

questions.q: A 28-year-old presents with a painless firm ulcer at the coronal sulcus with bilateral non-tender inguinal lymphadenopathy. VDRL is 1:16. He should be treated with:
opts: Benzathine penicillin 1.2 million units IM single dose
Benzathine penicillin 2.4 million units IM single dose
Procaine penicillin 600,000 units IM daily for 10 days
questions.exp: Primary syphilis (painless chancre + bilateral LAP + reactive VDRL) in a non-penicillin-allergic patient: Benzathine penicillin G 2.4 million units IM single dose is the treatment of choice. The 1.2 million unit dose is insufficient. Doxycycline 100mg BD for 14 days is used in penicillin allergy.

questions.q: A 45-year-old presents with flaccid blisters on the trunk and scalp. Nikolsky's sign is positive. Biopsy shows suprabasal acantholysis with 'tombstone' appearance of basal cells. The target antigen is:
questions.exp: Pemphigus vulgaris (PV) predominantly affects mucous membranes and trunk. DIF shows intercellular IgG (fish-net/chicken-wire pattern). The target antigen is Desmoglein 3 (mucosal type). Desmoglein 1 is the target in pemphigus foliaceus (superficial type, no mucosal involvement). Both in PV with skin+mucosa involvement.

questions.q: A 16-year-old presents with multiple comedones, papules, and pustules on the face. She also has tender nodules on the jaw line. What is the most appropriate treatment?
opts: Oral doxycycline + topical retinoid + benzoyl peroxide
questions.exp: Moderate-to-severe nodulocystic acne (nodules + multiple inflammatory lesions) is best managed with oral antibiotics (doxycycline/minocycline) + topical retinoid + benzoyl peroxide. This combination addresses C. acnes, inflammation, and comedones. Oral isotretinoin is reserved for severe nodulo-cystic acne unresponsive to conventional therapy or with scarring.

questions.q: A 55-year-old man presents with worsening pruritic plaques on the trunk and limbs. Biopsy shows epidermotropic infiltrate of atypical lymphocytes with cerebriform nuclei forming Pautrier's microabscesses. Immunophenotype: CD4+, CD7-, CD8-. The staging of his disease is primarily based on:
opts: Percentage of BSA involved + lymph node status + blood/visceral involvement
questions.exp: Mycosis fungoides (MF) — the most common cutaneous T-cell lymphoma (CTCL) — is staged using the TNM system: T (skin: BSA involved/type), N (lymph node), M (visceral), B (blood). The ISCL/EORTC staging is based on extent of skin involvement (patches, plaques, tumors), lymph node involvement, and blood/visceral involvement.

questions.q: A 25-year-old presents for a Mohs surgery on a BCC on the nose. The key advantage of Mohs micrographic surgery over wide local excision is:
opts: It does not require local anesthesia
Complete margin assessment with tissue conservation
It can be performed without histopathology
Lower recurrence rate on the trunk
questions.exp: Mohs micrographic surgery (MMS) involves sequential horizontal tissue removal with 100% margin control — the entire surgical margin is mapped and examined microscopically. This allows complete margin assessment while maximally conserving normal tissue, achieving the highest cure rates (99%+ for primary BCC) with the smallest defect, especially on anatomically critical areas like the nose.

questions.q: A 30-year-old presents with painful lymphadenopathy in the inguinal region and a healed genital ulcer. Aspiration of the buboes yields creamy pus. Frei test is positive. The causative organism belongs to serovars:
questions.exp: Lymphogranuloma venereum (LGV) is caused by Chlamydia trachomatis serovars L1, L2, L3. It presents with painless genital ulcer (heals quickly) followed by painful inguinal lymphadenopathy (bubo). Frei test (positive intracutaneous test) is now obsolete. Serovars A-C cause trachoma; D-K cause urogenital chlamydia. Treatment: doxycycline 100mg BD for 21 days.
